strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: building a unified multivariate time-series foundation model that can handle multiple generative tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) without task-specific architectural modifications.

The empirical observation that time series with different granularities exhibit distinct amplitude-frequency and phase-frequency joint distributions (Figures 1 and 3, Appendix A.4.1) is an interesting motivating analysis, and the design of granularity-aware Fourier attention modules follows from it coherently.

The autoregressive blank infilling pre-training strategy adapted from GLM is a reasonable unification of masked reconstruction and causal forecasting objectives, allowing a single output head to serve multiple generative tasks.

The experimental evaluation is fairly broad: long-term forecasting on 5 benchmarks with 4 horizons against 10 baselines, imputation at 4 missing ratios, anomaly detection on 5 datasets, plus pre-training effectiveness comparisons (Tables 5, 6, 8) and ablations of the frequency and granularity-aware components (Table 7).

Implementation details (hyperparameters, GPU configuration, dataset statistics) are reported in sufficient detail in Appendix A.2.3, and the authors honestly discuss limitations including the lack of unified benchmarks (Appendix A.6).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the model is largely an assembly of existing components (RevIN, channel independence, patching from PatchTST; FFT-based attention similar to FEDformer/FreTS/Fredformer; GLM-style blank infilling; low-rank adapter-like modules). The claimed 'first MTS foundation model to integrate Fourier Knowledge Attention' is a weak and somewhat circular novelty claim.

The central empirical finding is questionable as a 'finding': it is expected that different sampling granularities produce different frequency resolutions and thus different frequency-domain distributions. Moreover, the analysis in Figure 1 compares different datasets (with different granularities AND different domains), so the distribution differences cannot be causally attributed to granularity alone. A controlled analysis on the same series re-sampled at different rates is missing.

The granularity-aware design is crude: exactly five learnable key vectors (day/hour/minute/second/millisecond) with a quintuple time encoding hard-codes a limited granularity vocabulary, which does not match the actual pre-training data (e.g., 1ms-8ms health data, 20ms IoT data fall outside the millisecond resolution, and sub-daily irregularities are ignored). The paper does not analyze what the attention weights actually learn or whether granularity routing behaves as claimed.

Evaluation rigor concerns: (1) baseline numbers are copied from original papers rather than re-run under a unified protocol, which the authors themselves acknowledge is problematic; (2) strong recent multi-task baselines (Timer, MOIRAI, UniTS in full) are missing or partial in key tables; (3) anomaly detection uses the point-adjust protocol, which is known to severely inflate F1 scores and is discouraged by the community; (4) improvements in ablations are small (1-3%) and no statistical significance or seed variance is reported.

Despite positioning as a foundation model, there is no zero-shot or few-shot evaluation on unseen datasets, which is the standard test for foundation-model claims; the model is only evaluated after fine-tuning on the same well-known benchmarks used by prior task-specific work.
Reproducibility is uncertain: no code or pre-trained checkpoint release is mentioned, and pre-training on 6 A100 GPUs with 1B+ time points is non-trivial to reproduce.

The writing has numerous typos, grammatical errors, and inconsistencies that impede clarity ('devided', 'Paching', 'Pae-Frequency', 'the the first layer', duplicated 'electricity' row in Table 6, missing values and inconsistent columns in Tables 2 and 7, incorrect abbreviations like 'Ground Trues'). Several equations (e.g., Eq. 3) are imprecise regarding dimensions and the role of the low-rank modules, and Eq. 13 in the appendix defines a single bandwidth h = hx = hy, contradicting the 2-D Scott's rule description.

The paper does not evaluate classification despite Table 1 advertising UniTS's broader task coverage as a differentiator; GTM's own Table 1 shows it also cannot do classification, weakening the 'universal representation' narrative.

The abstract and conclusion claim GTM 'outperforms SOTA across all generative tasks,' but the results show GTM is second-best on Electricity (imputation and forecasting MSE in some settings) and behind PatchTST/TIME on several entries, so the claims are stronger than the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: unified, task-agnostic pre-training for multivariate time series foundation models covering forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection.

The core architectural idea — conditioning frequency-domain attention on time granularity (via a quintuple time-granularity embedding and low-rank Fourier knowledge modules) — is reasonably novel and is directly motivated by the proposed empirical analysis.

The evaluation covers three generative tasks with multiple baselines, and includes pre-training ablations (GTM vs. no-pretrain) and component ablations (w/o time granularity, w/o FFT), which is more thorough than many comparable submissions.

The autoregressive blank-infilling pre-training (adapted from GLM) with a unified output projection is a sensible design that plausibly removes token/model-level customizations for downstream generative tasks.
weaknesses: The central 'first principle' empirical finding is weak and arguably trivial: it is well known that sampling rate determines the Nyquist range and thus the frequency content of a signal, so observing distinct amplitude/phase-frequency joint distributions across granularities is expected a priori. Only four qualitative 3D KDE plots are shown, with no statistical testing, effect quantification, or control for confounds (e.g., different datasets dominate different granularity bins), yet the paper builds strong claims ('overlooked by all contemporary models') on this evidence. Prior work such as MOIRAI explicitly targets cross-frequency learning, undermining the novelty claim.

The methodology is under-specified and at times incoherent: Eq. 3 mixes five low-rank factors {A_i, B_i} with a full connection layer W_full in a way whose dimensions and interaction with the attention softmax are hard to verify; the 'knowledge attention' mechanism is compared to MoE only loosely; and it is unclear how frequency-domain modules actually improve generative quality rather than acting as extra capacity. No code release is mentioned, harming reproducibility.

Evaluation has significant inconsistencies and fairness concerns: (i) Table 2 contains missing entries (TTME has no MAE values; UniTS-PMT is absent on ETTm1), making some claimed wins unverifiable; (ii) strong recent foundation-model baselines (Timer, MOIRAI, TimesFM) are discussed in related work but not actually compared against on the main tasks; (iii) the claimed average F1 differs between Table 4 (87.01) and Table 8 (87.15); (iv) the anomaly detection protocol relies on the point-adjustment strategy, which is widely documented as severely inflating F1 scores, so the reported gains (often <1% over GPT4TS) may not be meaningful.

Improvements over baselines are modest and inconsistent: forecasting gains over PatchTST are marginal on several datasets (e.g., Electricity, Traffic), GTM is not best on PSM (Table 4) or Electricity imputation (Table 13), and pre-training contributes only 0.5-1.2% on Electricity/Traffic — casting doubt on whether the 'universal knowledge representation' story actually explains performance.

The paper overstates its scope: Table 1 advertises generality and 'no inference adaptation,' but classification is not evaluated, and fine-tuning is still required for anomaly detection and imputation; the claimed resolution of the 'last-mile' bottleneck is therefore only partially supported.

Writing quality is poor for a top-tier submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('devided', 'Paching', 'Phae-Frequency', 'fuction', 'GTP4TS', broken sentence in A.2.3), inconsistent notation (T used for both lookback and prediction length), and tables with formatting errors (duplicated 'electricity' row in Table 6). These issues reduce confidence in the overall rigor of the work.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three generative tasks (long-term forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) on widely used benchmark datasets, with extensive full results in the appendix.

The proposed model is architecturally coherent: combining temporal self-attention with a frequency-domain knowledge attention module conditioned on time granularity is a reasonable design, and the ablation studies (Table 7/16) provide evidence that both the frequency module and the granularity-aware attention contribute to performance.

The unified autoregressive blank-infilling pre-training strategy adapted from GLM is a sensible approach to making one model serve forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection without task-specific architectural changes, and the pre-training vs. no-pre-training comparison (Tables 5, 6, 8) supports the value of large-scale pre-training.
The related-work coverage is thorough, and Table 1 gives a clear positioning of GTM relative to prior time series foundation models.
Detailed implementation information (pre-training data statistics, hyperparameters, hardware) is provided, which helps assess reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central 'new empirical finding' (Section 1 / Figure 1) that time granularity changes the joint amplitude-frequency distribution is largely a consequence of Bearer [REDACTED] processing: changing the sampling rate necessarily changes the frequency support and resolution of the FFT. Presenting this as a novel, overlooked property of MTS data overstates the insight; the connection from this observation to the specific architecture (five fixed granularity keys S/MS/M/H/D) is weak and not formally established.

The scalability of the granularity encoding is a concern: the model hard-codes five granularity levels (second, millisecond, minute, hour, day). It is unclear how GTM handles granularities outside this set (weekly, monthly, yearly, irregular sampling), how the granularity query is selected at inference time, and whether the claim of 'universal' representation actually generalizes beyond the pre-training corpus.

Baseline comparisons largely cite reported numbers from prior papers rather than re-running methods under a unified protocol; the paper itself acknowledges the lack of unified benchmarks in Appendix A.6. This makes the headline 'GTM outperforms all SOTA models' claim difficult to verify fairly, and several relevant foundation models (e.g., Timer, MOMENT, Time-MOE) are absent from the main comparison tables despite being discussed in related work. Several table entries are missing ('-') without explanation.

Anomaly detection uses the point-adjust protocol, which recent literature has shown can drastically inflate F1 scores; using more faithful evaluation protocols (e.g., event-based F1 or affiliation metrics) would be needed to support the claimed gains. Additionally, Table 4 is incomplete (F2 column missing for GTM).

The evaluation lacks the standard foundation-model capability tests: no zero-shot or few-shot cross-domain evaluation, and no evaluation on predictive (classification) tasks, despite the framing as a 'universal knowledge representation' foundation model. The claim of universality is thus supported only by in-domain fine-tuned performance.

Novelty is largely a combination of existing components (PatchTST-style patching and channel independence, GLM blank infilling, FFT-based attention as in FEDformer/FreTS/FiTS); the Fourier Knowledge Attention module is the main novel element but its mechanism is described at a high level and several design choices (e.g., why five modules, why low-rank factorization with rank 385) are not justified.

Significant writing and presentation problems undermine clarity: multiple typos ('dived into', 'Paching', 'Phae-Frequency', 'in debating', 'the As we do'), broken/inconsistent table formatting (Table 2 header and misaligned rows), and incorrect internal references (e.g., 'Table6', 'Table14' referenced from Tables 5/6 inconsistently). These errors make careful checking of results difficult.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, which is important given the model is pre-trained from scratch on a 12G-token dataset and the authors themselves note the field lacks fair-comparison infrastructure.

Ablations are performed only on the forecasting task; it is unclear whether the frequency/granularity modules benefit imputation and anomaly detection, which would be needed to support the paper's universal-representation claim.

strengths: Comprehensive multi-task evaluation spanning forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification, with additional zero-shot/few-shot experiments, ablation studies, scaling-law analysis, and a detailed efficiency/latency breakdown—well beyond the typical evaluation depth for TSFM papers.

The empirical analysis of amplitude/phase-frequency joint distributions across temporal granularities (Figure 1, Appendix B.4.1) provides a motivated, data-driven rationale for the granularity-aware Fourier attention design.

The hybrid masking strategy unifying blank-infilling reconstruction and tail-masked autoregression is a reasonable adaptation of GLM-style pre-training to time series, and supports the task-agnostic adaptation story.

Results are competitive across benchmarks, including comparisons against recent TSFMs (Timer, MOIRAI, MOMENT, TimesFM, Sundial, Time-MOE) and evaluation on the more rigorous TSB-AD anomaly benchmark and two under-explored real-world datasets (PV, L2C).
Error-bar analysis with 95% CIs over 10 runs and thorough hyperparameter sensitivity analysis in the appendix strengthen reliability of reported numbers.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely combinatorial: FFT/iFFT-based attention is closely related to FEDformer, patching/CI to PatchTST, blank-infilling masking and 2D positional encoding directly to GLM, and span permutation to span-corruption schemes. The genuinely new element (five fixed granularity-key embeddings gating low-rank frequency modules) is a fairly heuristic design with a hard-coded quintuple (day/hour/minute/second/ms), and its benefit over simply conditioning on frequency content is not clearly isolated.

The claim of being 'the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM' is overstated and not rigorously defended; UniTS and Timer make overlapping claims, and GTM itself still modifies the projection head for classification and fine-tunes for anomaly detection. The boundary of 'task-agnostic' is never precisely defined.

Comparison fairness concerns: many baseline numbers are cited from original papers under potentially different settings rather than re-run; against the strongest same-scale TSFMs (Table 20), GTM actually loses to Time-MOE-Base and Sundial-Small on ETTh1 and ETTm1 average MSE, which softens the headline 'consistently outperforms SOTA' claim.

Ablation gains from the Fourier and granularity modules are modest (roughly 1–3% relative MSE), and the main anomaly detection table still relies on the point-adjustment protocol that the authors themselves cite as biased (Liu & Paparrizos, 2024), only moving to TSB-AD in the appendix.

The code repository link in the introduction is empty/incomplete, undermining reproducibility claims; there are also textual/typographical inconsistencies (e.g., garbled percentage annotations in Tables 24–26, an unfinished sentence 'available at:', 'GTP4TS' typo) suggesting insufficient polish.

The causal link from the KDE distribution analysis to architectural design is loose—Figure 1 shows distributions differ across granularities, but there is no direct evidence that the granularity-gated attention actually learns these distributions (no probing, attention visualization, or representation analysis).

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification), with additional zero-shot/few-shot, ablation, and scalability studies
The empirical analysis of joint amplitude/phase-frequency distributions across temporal granularities (Figure 1) is an interesting observation that motivates the design
The hybrid masking strategy unifying masked reconstruction and autoregressive forecasting is a reasonable engineering contribution, and results on standard benchmarks are competitive
Efficiency analysis (Table 9-11, 30) with latency breakdowns and heterogeneous hardware is a welcome addition
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core components are largely assembled from prior work — GLM blank infilling (hybrid masking, 2D positional encoding, span shuffling), patching/RevIN/channel independence from PatchTST, and frequency-domain attention echoing FEDformer/FiLM/FreTS/TimesNet. The 'Five learnable keys over a granularity quintuple' gating is a small design delta; the rank-1 low-rank frequency modules (A ∈ R^{385×1}, B ∈ R^{1×385}) raise questions about whether such capacity can meaningfully capture frequency-specific patterns

The claim of being 'the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM' is overstated: the model still requires removing masking/2D positional encoding for downstream tasks and replacing the projection head for classification. Existing seq2seq TSFMs (Timer, UP2ME, UniTS) already support multiple tasks without per-task retraining

Cherry-picked comparisons: in Table 20, Time-MOE-Base actually outperforms GTM on ETTh1 (0.379 vs 0.404 avg MSE) and many other cells, yet the text claims GTM 'slightly outperforms' based on best-count; in Table 5, TimesFM substantially beats GTM on ETTm1 (0.354 vs 0.593) zero-shot, but the narrative claims GTM ranks first. Baseline tables contain many missing entries (dashes), weakening the SOTA claim

Ablation gains are small and inconsistent (1-4% MSE), and the scalability study is modest (35M params, 12 layers) relative to the 'foundation model' framing; the paper's conclusion that width alone doesn't help suggests limited scaling evidence
Anomaly detection relies on the point-adjustment evaluation protocol, which is well known to be problematic and was criticized by the same TSB-AD benchmark (Liu & Paparrizos, 2024) the authors cite

Presentation issues undermine confidence: the code availability URL is left blank ('available at:'), multiple typos ('GTP4TS', 'Table25', 'the As we do', 'adapting to at the tail'), and Figure 1 KDE plots are unreadable at page scale
Efficiency claims are mixed: Table 9 shows GTM is slower at inference than Time-MOE and GPT-2 and uses much more training memory, which is glossed over as 'competitive'

strengths: The paper is ambitious in scope: GTM targets forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification with a single pre-trained model and a single output projection, and the claim of task-agnostic generative adaptation is a meaningful goal for the TSFM literature.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: 5 forecasting datasets with 4 horizons, imputation at 4 missing ratios, 5 anomaly detection datasets plus the more rigorous TSB-AD benchmark, 10 classification datasets, zero-shot/few-shot comparisons, pre-training ablations, data/model scaling studies, and latency/efficiency profiling — more thorough than typical for this area.
Error bar analysis (10 trials, 95% CIs) and efficiency breakdowns (FFT/Fourier attention overhead, parameter/memory/speed trade-offs) add rigor and are commendable.
The Fourier attention ablation (complete vs. w/o granularity vs. w/o frequency) is directionally consistent with the paper's hypothesis about granularity-aware frequency representations.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The 'Fourier attention' is essentially frequency-domain mixing as in FEDformer, augmented with a small granularity-conditioned gating over five rank-1 low-rank matrices; the hybrid masking is GLM blank infilling (Du et al., 2022) with a tail-masking knob; the tokenization pipeline (RevIN + CI + patching) is standard from PatchTST. The paper should more clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond recombination.

Claims of 'consistently outperforms SOTA' are overclaimed. Table 20 shows Time-MOE-Base clearly beats GTM on ETTh1 (0.379 vs 0.404 avg MSE) and Sundial is competitive; Table 3 anomaly detection wins over GPT4TS by only 0.33% on average with GTM losing on MSL, SMD, and PSM; classification results are mixed (e.g., JapaneseVowels 92.1 vs. 98.6 for GPT4TS). A fairer framing of parity/mixed results is needed.

The central motivating analysis (Figure 1) is descriptive and thin: FFT + 2D KDE density plots differing across granularities is expected, and the leap from this observation to exactly five granularity keys (day/hour/minute/second/ms) and a quintuple encoding is heuristic and under-justified. The ablation shows the granularity module contributes only ~1–3% MSE on top of the frequency module.

Technical presentation has gaps: Eq. (3) is ambiguous about how per-patch column-wise FFT, rank-1 modules (A ∈ R^{385×1}, B ∈ R^{1×385}), and the always-on global module interact with the temporal attention output; the claim that granularity-aware attention operates across channels given Channel Independence is unexplained; how granularity quintuples are obtained for arbitrary datasets at inference is unclear.

Table 3 uses the point-adjustment protocol, which has been shown to inflate F1 substantially (a concern the authors themselves acknowledge when citing Liu & Paparrizos, 2024); the non-adjusted TSB-AD results in the appendix partially address this but the headline table does not.
Zero-shot evaluation is narrow (5 datasets, horizon 96 only) and mixed — GTM loses to TimesFM on ETTm1 and Traffic; the 'average MSE first' summary hides this.

Reproducibility concerns: the code availability statement is literally blank in the manuscript ('The code and implementation details are available at:'), several baselines use cited numbers rather than uniform reproduction, and baseline selection criteria vary across tasks.

Writing quality issues (e.g., 'Apply a controlled proportion of consecutive [MASK] tokens to at the tail', 'pad learnable vectors [START] and [END] tokens', inconsistent formatting) and some table inconsistencies (Table 8 average annotation) suggest the paper needs another careful pass.

The 'first generative-task-agnostic TSFM' novelty claim is debatable given Timer/UniTS also handle multiple generative tasks with unified objectives; the differentiation rests on fine-grained implementation choices rather than a clearly delineated capability gap.
